query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 6 at% aluminum to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of nanoscale, coherent L12-type precipitates that enhance dispersion strengthening, thereby improving the alloy’s elevated-temperature yield strength relative to the same alloy without the aluminum addition.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy containing at least three additional elements, each within the 5–35 at% range, processed via homogenization to ensure even elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Incorporate approximately 6 at% aluminum into the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy and subject the material to a homogenization heat treatment followed by solution treatment.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing (around 800 °C) under a controlled, inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent L12-type (Ni3Al-like) precipitates formed during the specified heat treatments.
generation.mechanism: The aluminum addition triggers the formation of coherent precipitates that act as barriers to dislocation motion, thereby improving yield strength via dispersion strengthening at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-doped alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength compared to the baseline alloy without aluminum, although the precise magnitude of enhancement remains to be confirmed.
generation.baseline: An identical titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy composition fabricated without the aluminum addition.
generation.boundary: The intervention applies to high-entropy alloys where all constituent elements remain between 5–35 at% and where processing conditions (homogenization and solution treatment) are optimized to promote L12 precipitate formation. Testing is focused on elevated temperatures around 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: While a significant strengthening effect is predicted based on dispersion strengthening from L12 precipitates, the exact percentage improvement in yield strength (e.g., the target of around 15% or more) is uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of baseline titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without aluminum and one set with an addition of approximately 6 at% aluminum. Both sets should be processed identically using homogenization and solution treatment. Perform mechanical testing at 800 °C under an inert atmosphere along with microstructural analysis.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength from tensile tests
Creep resistance from constant-load creep testing
X-ray diffraction for phase identification of L12-type precipitates
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess precipitate size, distribution, and coherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-doped samples do not exhibit a measurable improvement in yield strength or creep resistance at 800 °C relative to the baseline alloy—or if the expected L12-type precipitates are not observed in the microstructural analysis—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Substituting 5 at% of one minor alloying element with zirconium in a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of fine, thermally stable Zr-containing precipitates that pin grain boundaries and obstruct dislocation motion, thereby improving elevated‐temperature yield strength and creep resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy consisting of approximately 30 at% Ti, 30 at% Ni, and three other elements each present between 5 and 35 at% (with none being zirconium) processed as per standard processing for high-entropy alloys.
drafts.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by replacing 5 at% of one of the minor alloying elements with zirconium. This substitution is performed while keeping all other overall compositional criteria within the high-entropy regime.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is processed under identical conditions (e.g., solution treatment followed by an aging step at a temperature near 0.7–0.8 times the melting temperature) to promote fine precipitate formation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Fine-scale, thermally stable Zr-containing precipitates distributed along grain boundaries and within grains, leading to a refined microstructure.
drafts.mechanism: Zirconium has a high affinity for forming stable intermetallic phases. Its controlled addition encourages the precipitation of Zr-rich phases during aging, which act as barriers to dislocation movement and help pin grain boundaries, thus retarding grain growth and delaying creep deformation at elevated temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The zirconium-modified alloy will exhibit superior elevated-temperature mechanical properties (notably enhanced yield strength and improved creep resistance at temperatures above approximately 700°C) relative to the identical baseline alloy lacking zirconium.
drafts.baseline: Titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with the same overall composition and processing route but without the zirconium substitution.
drafts.boundary: The intervention applies to high-entropy alloys where all constituent elements remain between 5–35 at% and under processing conditions optimized for precipitate formation (e.g., specific heat treatment schedules). The operating environment must involve elevated temperatures (e.g., 700°C or higher) relevant to extreme environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the high-entropy alloy: one with the standard composition (control) and one with 5 at% zirconium substitution for one minor element (test). Subject both batches to an identical heat treatment regimen optimized for precipitate formation. Perform elevated-temperature mechanical testing (including tensile and creep tests at temperatures above 700°C) and microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM and XRD) to document precipitate formation and grain boundary characteristics.
measurements: Creep resistance (e.g., time-to-failure under constant load)
Grain size and precipitate distribution from microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the zirconium-substituted alloy fails to show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the control, or if microstructural analysis reveals detrimental secondary phases compromising performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding ~6 at% aluminum to a Ti–Ni-primary high-entropy alloy (with 3+ other elements also at 5–35 at% each) induces L12-type (Ni3Al-like) precipitates that strengthen the matrix at elevated temperatures, resulting in higher yield strength compared to a similar alloy without the aluminum addition.
drafts.material_initial_state: A baseline Ti–Ni-primary high-entropy alloy containing at least three other elements (each at 5–35 at%) and prepared via vacuum arc melting, with all elements homogenized at elevated temperature.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate approximately 6 at% Al into the baseline Ti–Ni-primary high-entropy alloy, then homogenize at ∼1200 °C for 24 hours and perform a solution treatment (e.g., 1000 °C for 2 hours) followed by water quenching.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature stress testing at or above 800 °C under a controlled, inert atmosphere to assess mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength, creep resistance).
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent L12 Ni3Al-type precipitates formed within the alloy matrix during homogenization and solution treatment.
drafts.mechanism: The coherent Ni3Al-like precipitates provide dispersion strengthening: their formation and distribution resist dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby improving high-temperature performance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase (e.g., ≥15%) in elevated-temperature (≥800 °C) yield strength relative to the baseline alloy without Al addition.
drafts.baseline: An identical Ti–Ni-primary high-entropy alloy composition without Al.
drafts.boundary: Applies to Ti–Ni-primary high-entropy alloys with overall compositions still within the 5–35 at% element range. Formation of the L12 precipitates is contingent on appropriate homogenization and solution treatments.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce baseline and 6 at% Al-doped Ti–Ni-primary high-entropy alloy ingots following identical melting and homogenization protocols, then perform high-temperature mechanical tests (at 800 °C) and microstructural analysis.
measurements: X-ray diffraction to identify L12 Ni3Al-type precipitates
TEM-based precipitate size and distribution analysis
High-temperature yield strength measurements in tension
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped samples do not exhibit increased yield strength (≥15%) or if they fail to show the expected Ni3Al-type precipitates, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small concentration (1–3 at%) of hafnium (Hf) into a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties by enhancing grain boundary strengthening and stabilizing the microstructure at high temperatures.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy primarily composed of titanium and nickel, with other elements meeting the 5–35 at% compositional definition.
drafts.intervention: Addition of 1–3 at% hafnium to the alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: Elevated-temperature environments (e.g., 800–1000°C) relevant to extreme applications such as aerospace or power generation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Grain boundary strengthening and microstructural stabilization due to hafnium's high melting point and strong affinity for forming stable intermetallic phases.
drafts.mechanism: Hafnium atoms segregate to grain boundaries, reducing grain boundary mobility and enhancing resistance to creep and grain coarsening at high temperatures. Additionally, hafnium may form stable intermetallic phases that impede dislocation motion, further improving mechanical strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The alloy with hafnium will exhibit higher yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the same alloy without hafnium.
drafts.baseline: The elevated-temperature mechanical properties of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without hafnium.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys with 5–35 at% of other elements and tested in the 800–1000°C temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy samples, one with 1–3 at% hafnium and one without. Subject both sets to tensile and creep tests at 800–1000°C.
measurements: Microstructural analysis of grain boundaries and intermetallic phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of hafnium does not result in a measurable improvement in yield strength or creep resistance, or if no evidence of grain boundary strengthening or microstructural stabilization is observed, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of carbon (1-3 at%) into a titanium-nickel high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the same alloy without carbon.
drafts.material_initial_state: Titanium-nickel high-entropy alloy without carbon addition.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of carbon-rich precipitates that improve strength and ductility.
drafts.mechanism: Carbon acts as a solid solution strengthener and promotes the formation of beneficial microstructural features that enhance mechanical properties at elevated temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The titanium-nickel-carbon high-entropy alloy will exhibit improved yield strength and ductility at elevated temperatures compared to the titanium-nickel alloy without carbon.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to titanium-nickel alloys with 1-3 at% carbon and tested at elevated temperatures above 600°C.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct mechanical tests (tensile and compression) on both the titanium-nickel alloy with and without carbon addition at elevated temperatures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the titanium-nickel-carbon alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength or ductility compared to the titanium-nickel alloy without carbon, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Addition of a refractory element such as molybdenum to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy improves its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
drafts.material_initial_state: Titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with 5-35 at% of each primary constituent and additional elements to meet the high-entropy alloy definition.
drafts.intervention: Addition of 5-15 at% molybdenum to the alloy composition.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a solid solution with refined grain structure and precipitation of intermetallic phases.
drafts.mechanism: The refractory element molybdenum enhances the alloy's heat resistance and specific strength by forming a solid solution that reduces grain boundary sliding and promotes the precipitation of intermetallic phases, which act as obstacles to dislocation movement.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the alloy without molybdenum addition.
drafts.baseline: Titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without molybdenum addition.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with and without 10 at% molybdenum addition using tensile testing and creep testing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with molybdenum addition shows no significant improvement in yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, or creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the alloy without molybdenum, the hypothesis is falsified.
